$comment: The inward-only dependency rule, written so a machine can check it.
Tech-Stack-Plan.md 4.2 owns the rule itself; this file is its executable form and must
not drift from it. Widening a mayInclude list is a licensing-grade decision about the
architecture -- make it here, in a diff, with a reason in the commit message.
Layers are matched by path prefix, longest first, so core/settings/ can carry different
permissions from core/ without depending on JSON key order.
$comment-extensions: `.def` was added at T9, closing a hole that had been open since T3. An X-macro table is
#included straight into a translation unit, so an #include inside one lands in the including
layer exactly as if it had been written there -- and until this line, layer-lint could not see
it. Four such tables exist (ActionId.def, KeyBindingDefaults.def, SettingsKeys.def,
ShellKeys.def) and every one of them is included by a layer with a deny list. Whether a file
is COMPILED is a fact about the build; whether it is part of a layer is what this gate is for.
$comment-exclude: tests/gates/fixtures/ holds files that are violations BY CONSTRUCTION -- that is what
they test. Excluding them by an explicit path (decision D0-4) rather than by a filename
convention means the exclusion is greppable and shows up in --explain. A convention like
'*_bad.cpp' would silently stop testing the first fixture that forgot the suffix.
third_party/ is fetched, not committed (scripts/fetch-pdfium.ps1), so without this entry
the scanned set depends on whether a developer has run that script: 27 files on a fresh
clone, 51 once PDFium is present. The gate's own report must not vary with machine state.
Nothing was being checked there in any case -- third-party files match no layer, and
LayerLint skips unlayered files before any include or token rule runs.

app.note: app/ is the composition root -- the only place that may name a concrete backend or platform. It holds no domain logic.

ui.note: ui/ may never include pdf/ or platform/win/, and may never mutate a Document: its entire mutation vocabulary is to construct a Command and hand it to CommandJournal. TWO SINGLE-FILE EXCEPTIONS, each of which is an INTERFACE header with its own layer entry constraining what it may contain: platform/platform.h, whose own header comment has always said it is included by core/, ui/ and app/ (the omission here was a gap found at T9, not a widening); and app/Services.h, the aggregate of injected interfaces that Architecture-FileMap.md 3.1 names ui/shell/MainWindow and ui/shell/DocumentWindow as the consumers of.

app-services.note: app/Services.h is the composition root's INTERFACE header, and it is ui/'s one permitted look outward. So it is constrained the way platform/platform.h is: it may name core/ types and platform::Platform and nothing else. Without this entry, a pdf/ include added to Services.h at Stage 2 would silently give every widget that consumes it a dependency on the PDF engine -- which is the exact coupling the layer split exists to prevent, arriving through the one file allowed to cross.

platform-interface.note: platform/platform.h is INTERFACES ONLY and is included by core/, ui/ and app/. An OS header reaching it gives all three a platform-SDK dependency -- min/max macros, `interface`, GetMessage renaming itself -- and the failure would not show up here: it would show up as the Linux portable-asan job no longer being able to build core/, which is the mechanical proof that the domain layer is portable. A Win32 handle crosses this boundary as an opaque integer, and nothing else does.

core-backend.note: core/backend.h is the ENGINE boundary -- INTERFACES ONLY, and it is included by core/, pdf/, ui/ and app/. It gets its own entry for the reason platform/platform.h has one, and Stage2-Rendering-Plan.md 10 calls for it by name: a PDFium header or an FPDF_ symbol reaching this file would hand all four layers a dependency on the engine through the one door that is open, and the failure would surface not here but as the Linux portable-asan job no longer being able to build core/. What crosses this boundary is BUFFERS AND CALLBACKS -- which is also why QImage is denied and IPageRasterizer hands back a RasterImage instead: core/ may not name a QtGui type, and ui/ wraps the bytes at the far side. Note that it may include core/ and NOT platform/platform.h: this header is the engine contract and has no business naming the OS boundary.

core-settings.note: core/settings/ is core/ with one added privilege: it is the only part of core/ permitted to write to the filesystem.

core.note: core/ is the domain layer: std, QtCore, a short pure-computation allowlist (ICU, HarfBuzz, Hunspell), and its two interface headers. It must build and pass its full test suite with no display and no PDF engine linked.

pdf.note: pdf/ is the only layer that may emit PDF bytes or call FPDF_. It implements core/backend.h and does not know ui/ exists.

platform.note: platform/win/ implements platform/platform.h and nothing else. It makes no policy decisions.

$comment-external: denyExternal is a DENY list, not an allowlist, and that is deliberate. An allowlist
would have to enumerate the entire C++ standard library, and would fail closed every
time somebody used a header nobody had listed -- which teaches people to edit this file
to get their work done, and a rules file that is edited casually stops meaning anything.
The deny list names what must never appear. The linker enforces the remainder: core/
links only Qt6::Core, so an errant QtWidgets include fails to link even if it slips

tokenRules.message: Only pdf/ may name the PDFium C API. Everything else reaches the engine through core/backend.h, which is what keeps the engine replaceable and core/ testable with no engine linked.

Nothing in RawPage may read a path out of argv (issue I-04). argv is NARROW: the CRT transcodes the wide command line through the process ANSI code page, and anything the code page cannot represent becomes '?' -- lossily and irreversibly. Measured at T1 on this machine (ACP 950): an emoji path arrived as report-?????.pdf in argv while QCoreApplication::arguments(), which Qt sources from GetCommandLineW(), was byte-perfect. Parse QCoreApplication::arguments() instead. app/main.cpp is the one exception: it hands argv to QApplication and prints it for the --print-args measurement, which is the case that established the rule.

$comment: DECISION D1-7(a) -- the STATIC half of `nothing is wired directly to a widget slot`.
Every user action in RawPage is a named ActionId, and ribbon, QAT, context menus, chords,
the tool finder, the CLI and the batch runner all resolve to one and call
ActionRegistry::dispatch. That is what makes the headless batch runner (flow K, Stage 14)
able to reach every feature without a second implementation of any of them -- and it is
why a feature reachable only from a widget is unfinished rather than done.
A bare QAction is how that rule is broken, and it is broken invisibly: the button works.
So construction is confined to ui/shell/ActionFactory.cpp, which routes every action
through the registry, and to ui/shell/RawPageAction.h, which is the subclass definition
and therefore the one place that must name QAction as a base.
FIVE SPELLINGS, not one. Stage 0's third S1 (its own I-15) was a gate that passed real
violations because every fixture used the same spelling, so this rule carries the stack
declaration, the heap construction, the base-class initialiser and BOTH addAction()
conveniences that build an action for you -- QMenu's and QToolBar's -- and there is a
fixture for each.
NOT ESCAPABLE. There is no inline waiver marker, because there is no second legitimate
place: a file that needs an action asks ActionFactory for one. The one genuine exception --
a QMenu item that is navigation rather than a command, which Qt makes a QAction whether we
like it or not -- is served by ActionFactory::addNonCommandMenuItem, so it lives inside the
allowed path and is stamped for the runtime check rather than carved out here.
AND IT IS ONLY HALF THE MECHANISM. The lint catches the construction at the moment it is
written; it structurally cannot see a SECOND connect() added later to a legitimately
created action. That is what ActionFactory::wiringComplaints checks at show time (D1-7(b)),
and neither half alone suffices.
tokenRules.message: Only ui/shell/ActionFactory.cpp may construct a QAction (D1-7). Every action must be a RawPageAction carrying its ActionId, with exactly one receiver on triggered, dispatching through ActionRegistry -- that is what makes the command reachable from the CLI and the Stage 14 batch runner as well as from the button. Ask ActionFactory::create(). A menu item that is genuinely NOT a command goes through ActionFactory::addNonCommandMenuItem().

Writing to disk is confined to pdf/ (which owns the file format) and core/settings/ (which owns configuration), so that every byte reaching a user's document goes through the mutation pipeline. If a write here is genuinely correct, waive it inline with  // layer-lint: allow-filesystem-write(reason)  -- every waiver is listed by --explain.

$comment-tokens: Qt's write APIs are matched by the OPEN MODE, not by the class: QFile is the idiomatic
way to write a file and also the idiomatic way to read one, so matching 'QFile' alone
would flag every read in ui/ and bury the rule in waivers. QIODevice::WriteOnly and its
siblings appear only when something is being opened for writing. Before this the list
had no Qt write at all beyond QSaveFile, so the most obvious spelling of the violation
The filesystem-write rule is a HEURISTIC: it matches substrings on the code part of a
line, so it can miss a write behind a helper and can flag a mention that is not one.
That is why it is the only escapable rule. If the waivers ever number more than a
handful, the rule is wrong and should be narrowed -- an unusable gate gets switched off,
which is worse than a narrow one that stays on.
tools/ and tests/ are allowed to write because they are not product code: license-audit
generates THIRD-PARTY.md, and the test harness writes fixtures and diff images.
